title: The Middle-Length, closed
hook: from the root of all things to the training of the senses

segments.voice: Yesterday: sutta, and your line, yours. Which image did you tell someone about? Today we close the whole Middle-Length collection. Day five hundred twenty-one.

The first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings ends on a strange note. The text says the monks did not delight in what the Buddha had said about the root of all things. It doesn't say why. The last discourse ends with a young brahmin sitting silent and a quiet teaching about eyes that stay open. In between, a hundred and fifty more. Today, the whole shelf, from the first to the last. Today: the Middle-Length, closed.
screen: `THE FIRST: THE MONKS WERE NOT PLEASED.` → `THE LAST: EYES THAT STAY OPEN.` → `A HUNDRED AND FIFTY IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: The Pali name is Majjhima Nikaya: the middle collection. Middle here means middle-length. Not as long as the long discourses, not as short as the connected ones. It's arranged in three groups of fifty, the root fifty, the middle fifty and the last fifty, and the last group has two extra, which is how you get a hundred and fifty-two. Here's the road we walked. The root of all things, and all the taints. Heirs in dhamma, not in things. Fear met in the forest at night. The stained cloth that won't take the dye. The saw, and goodwill even under it. The water snake and the raft. Relay chariots. The noble search. Milk and water. Saccaka sweating. Examine even the teacher. Rahula and the mirror, then the earth. Angulimala, read whole. Any wood makes fire. Breathing in sixteen steps. A hall empty of elephants. One fine night. Punna going west. Rahula freed under a tree, six sets of six, and finally, seeing without being swept. Now here's the small surprise in the name. Majjhima is the same word as the middle in the middle way, majjhima patipada, the path between indulgence and self-torment that the Buddha named in his first teaching. The title is about length, not doctrine. But the collection keeps showing that path anyway: not grabbing, not pushing away, not shutting the eyes, not drowning in what they see. A hundred and fifty-two ways of walking down the middle, in words.
screen: `MAJJHIMA: THE MIDDLE COLLECTION` · `THREE FIFTIES, PLUS TWO` · `FROM THE ROOT TO THE SENSES` · `THE SAME WORD AS THE MIDDLE WAY` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE WAY, IN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one line. Choose one from the whole collection, whichever comes: the raft is for crossing. All of it changing. Empty of this. See and stay. Say it once, quietly, and then let it go silent. When the mind wanders, bring back just the line, and then the quiet again. Not grabbing it, not pushing it away. The bell holds the time.
The Middle-Length. The Majjhima Nikaya, a hundred and fifty-two discourses, from the root of all things to the training of the senses. Today's word.

Your line: the middle way, in words. Today, when you're pulled toward too much or too little, look for the middle, and remember a hundred and fifty-two discourses looking for it too. Day five hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: The Majjhima Nikaya is one of the five collections of the Sutta Pitaka in the Pali Canon, studied and recited in Theravada monasteries; many of its discourses have parallels in the Chinese Madhyama Agama, preserved by another early school.

original.note: Pali majjhima: middle. Majjhima Nikaya, the middle-length collection; majjhima patipada, the middle way.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Middle-Length Sayings are about the middle way.
what it means: the title means middle-length, between the long and the short collections.
what a scholar hears: the same adjective, majjhima, names the middle way in the first sermon, and a parallel collection, the Madhyama Agama, survives in Chinese translation from another early school.
